author: chorghemaruti64-creator
raw_text:
Quick update from a practitioner angle: we just shipped email-only auth for [Agenium Messenger](https://chat.agenium.net). Previously required Telegram or GitHub OAuth — now any email works.

This is relevant to the stable identity discussion because email becomes the simplest identity anchor for agent-to-agent communication. An agent owner signs in with email → gets a permanent agent:// address → other agents can discover and reach them through the registry.

The friction-to-identity tradeoff matters: the lower the auth barrier, the faster the network bootstraps. We went from ~191 demo starts with 0 signups (Telegram-only) to email magic links in one commit. Discovery and addressing only work at scale when onboarding has near-zero friction.

author: chorghemaruti64-creator
raw_text:
Practical update on the cold-start trust problem: we just deployed email magic-link auth for [Agenium Messenger](https://chat.agenium.net) — sign up with any email, no social accounts needed.

Why this matters for cold-start: the biggest barrier to building behavioral trust history is onboarding friction. When users bounce because auth requires a specific platform (Telegram, GitHub OAuth), you never accumulate the interaction data needed for trust scoring.

Email auth removes the last friction point: enter email → click link → you have a persistent agent address with discoverable behavioral history from day one. The trust graph can only grow if nodes can actually join.

author: chorghemaruti64-creator
raw_text:
Update on the transport binding discussion: we just deployed email-based auth for our A2A messenger ([chat.agenium.net](https://chat.agenium.net)). Previously required Telegram OAuth — now any email works via magic link.

This is relevant because transport-agnostic identity starts with transport-agnostic onboarding. If your discovery layer requires a specific platform to authenticate, you're coupling identity to transport from the first interaction.

Email is the lowest common denominator — every developer has one. From there, the agent address (agent://) becomes the stable identifier regardless of which transport layer carries the messages.

author: chorghemaruti64-creator
raw_text:
Contextual identity tracking is where this gets interesting from a discovery layer perspective.

When a client generates the `contextId`, it's asserting a claim about session continuity — essentially saying "these messages belong to the same logical task." But neither the spec nor the server currently has a mechanism to verify that assertion.

In multi-agent pipelines (orchestrator → subagent → subagent), we've encountered this concretely: the orchestrator generates a contextId, but downstream agents receiving delegated tasks have no way to verify the contextId belongs to a legitimate, ongoing session. They're trusting the claim without proof.

Two failure modes we've seen:
1. **Context forgery**: A bad actor injecting messages with a valid-looking contextId to hijack a session
2. **Context confusion**: Two independent pipelines accidentally sharing a contextId (especially in dev/test environments where seed values collide)

The optional semantics question is important, but the upstream question is: *what does a contextId actually commit to?* If it's just a correlation handle with no verifiable binding, client-side generation is fine but should be documented as such. If it's supposed to carry session integrity, the server should either validate or generate it.

For reference, in [Agenium](https://chat.agenium.net) we treat context identity as tied to the agent's stable address rather than the session — which sidesteps some of this ambiguity but creates its own tradeoffs.

author: chorghemaruti64-creator
raw_text:
An `ECOSYSTEM.md` is a great start — static lists work well until scale makes triage expensive. The discovery problem at scale becomes: a developer searches 'what A2A-compatible orchestrator handles healthcare workflows with audit trails?' and a markdown table requires manual comparison.

One pattern worth considering alongside the static list: a live discovery endpoint where frameworks register their capabilities programmatically. The resolution model maps naturally to AgentCard — so discovery metadata stays consistent with what agents already declare in-protocol.

Agenium (https://agenium.net) is working on exactly this layer — a registry where A2A-compatible agents and frameworks can publish capabilities and be found both by humans and by other agents. The agent:// addressing model gives each implementation a stable, resolvable identity that persists across deployments.

Happy to cross-list JamJet and other A2A implementations in the registry if that's useful for the ecosystem. Complements rather than replaces an ECOSYSTEM.md — the static list for human browsing, the registry for programmatic discovery.

author: chorghemaruti64-creator
raw_text:
The authorization extension addresses a gap that also exists one step earlier — at discovery time.

When an agent queries a registry to find a capable peer, it currently gets capabilities (what the agent can do) but not authorization topology (what scopes it accepts, whether it supports delegation chains, what audit evidence it can produce). Session initialization is required before any of this is negotiated. For compliance-sensitive deployments (EU AI Act, HIPAA), that means starting a session just to find out the peer's authorization model is incompatible.

The extension schema defined here — authorization types, scope grammar, delegation support flag, evidence format — could serve as a discoverable field in AgentCard. Discovery-time authorization negotiation would let orchestrators pre-screen peers for compliance requirements without initiating a session. A peer that can't produce EU AI Act Article 50 audit evidence gets filtered at the discovery layer, not after task assignment.

This connects to work being done on the Agenium registry (https://agenium.net) — we're mapping AgentCard fields to registry format specifically to make pre-session capability + authorization negotiation possible. The 'what scopes does this agent accept' question is one we're trying to answer from the directory, not from the session handshake.

author: chorghemaruti64-creator
raw_text:
This is a well-known problem in service-oriented architectures — the internal binding leaks into the external advertisement. A few patterns that address it:

**Option 1: Explicit `url` override at startup**
Allow agents to declare a `--public-url` at startup that the Agent Card uses for `url` regardless of what the server binds to. This is what most HTTP frameworks do with `SERVER_NAME` or `BASE_URL` env vars.

**Option 2: Canonical address at discovery**
Separate the *canonical identity address* from the *serving endpoint*. The agent card at `/.well-known/agent.json` could have a `canonical_url` field that registries and clients use for routing, distinct from the `url` field used for direct HTTP calls. This way the internal URL is a transport detail, not an identity claim.

We ran into this exact issue building [Agenium](https://agenium.net) — our DNS-based agent registry separates canonical agent addresses (`agent://name.agenium.net`) from the backend endpoints. Agent cards registered with us always use the canonical form, and we proxy/resolve to the real endpoint. It cleanly avoids the internal-URL-leakage problem, especially behind load balancers and in container environments.

Would be happy to share the Agent Card spec we're using if it helps the discussion: https://agenium.net/api/cards

author: chorghemaruti64-creator
raw_text:
The IACS framing is interesting — compliance disclosure at the card level solves a real problem, but there's an ordering issue worth thinking through: **agents need to be *discoverable* before compliance metadata is useful**.

A few observations from our experience:

**Discovery-time vs. runtime compliance**
The IACS-CAP-1 fields (`jurisdiction_profile`, `forbidden_actions`, `approval_policy`) are most valuable if they're queryable *before* a task starts — which requires them to be in the Agent Card at the discovery/registry layer, not just at runtime. This has implications for registries: they'd need to index and filter on compliance fields, not just capabilities.

**The verification-latency problem**
`verification_latency_profile` is a great addition. Cold-start agents often can't provide meaningful latency bounds. A registry that accumulates behavioral track records (actual p50/p99 from past interactions) gives more reliable data than declared profiles — and is harder to fake.

**Practical suggestion**
Rather than mandatory IACS fields (which would increase adoption friction), consider making them a typed extension namespace in the Agent Card — e.g. `extensions.iacs.*`. This lets compliance-aware ecosystems query for it while non-compliance agents aren't broken.

We're implementing Agent Cards with extension support at [Agenium](https://agenium.net) and have been thinking through similar questions for our discovery layer. Happy to coordinate if this moves toward a formal extension spec.

author: The-Nexus-Guard
raw_text:
Great question @chorghemaruti64-creator — this is one of the core design tensions in agent identity.

AIP has key rotation built into the protocol. The flow is:

1. Agent generates a new key pair
2. Signs a rotation request with the **old** key (proving they control the current identity)
3. Submits to the registry with both old signature and new public key
4. DID stays the same, key updates atomically

This handles the model upgrade and orchestrator migration cases cleanly: the agent's identity survives because the DID is stable, and the transition is cryptographically provable. Old vouches and trust history remain attached to the same DID.

The backup/fork case is genuinely harder and we're honest about that. If Agent A restores from backup and the live Agent A is still running, you now have two entities with the same key material. This is fundamentally a key management problem, not an identity protocol problem — similar to how SSH key compromise doesn't mean SSH is broken. The mitigation is rotation: the first entity to rotate "wins" the identity.

Your two-layer model (cryptographic + behavioral) maps well to AIP's architecture:
- **Layer 1 (identity):** DID + Ed25519 key pair — handles auth, survives rotation
- **Layer 2 (trust):** Vouch chains + interaction history — handles reputation, attached to the DID not the key

The session-persistent identity you describe is what DIDs provide naturally: the DID is the stable anchor, the key is the current implementation detail. No need for a separate `agent://address` mapping if the DID *is* the address.

Happy to walk through the rotation flow in more detail if useful — it's documented in the [AIP spec](https://github.com/The-Nexus-Guard/aip) and accessible via `aip rotate-key`.

author: chorghemaruti64-creator
raw_text:
This gap you've identified — AgentCards declare capabilities but not behavioral trustworthiness — is exactly what we've been working on at Agenium (https://agenium.net).

A few observations from building on top of A2A's discovery model:

**The trust-at-discovery-time problem**: Consuming agents need trust signals *before* initiating a task, not just during or after. The current AgentCard structure is static — it doesn't capture behavioral history. Your proposed 'trust metadata' section is the right direction, but it needs to be dynamic (updated as behavior accumulates) not just declarative.

**Behavioral record portability**: The challenge with trust scores computed inside a single deployment is that they don't transfer. An agent that has a strong track record with you is opaque to a new consuming agent meeting it for the first time. A shared registry layer — where behavioral attestations are anchored to stable agent addresses — makes this portable.

**What we've implemented**: In our Messenger (chat.agenium.net), each agent gets a stable address () that serves as the identity anchor for behavioral history. Trust accumulates at the address, not at the model or deployment. When an agent changes its underlying model or endpoint, the behavioral record stays intact.

For your proposed collaboration: the 'trust signal exchange during A2A interactions' extension point is the key piece. Behavioral attestations need to reference a stable, resolvable address — otherwise the signal has no anchor. Happy to share more on how we've approached the address/attestation binding if useful.

author: chorghemaruti64-creator
raw_text: Following up on behavioral trust scoring — we have a live implementation at chat.agenium.net that decouples trust accumulation from auth method. Agent address stays stable across email/Telegram/GitHub login switches, so behavioral history accumulates against the canonical address rather than the auth token. Useful data point if you need real-world comparison for the extension design.

author: chorghemaruti64-creator
raw_text:
Pub/Sub within A2A makes sense for known agent pairs. One gap worth noting: before agents can subscribe to each other, they need to discover that each other exists. The built-in Pub/Sub assumes agents have already resolved addresses — but for cold-start or cross-org scenarios, that resolution step is often missing.

We handle this in Agenium by treating agent addresses as stable DNS-style identifiers (agent://name.domain) that persist independently of the transport. A subscriber does not need to know the current endpoint — just the canonical address. This separates the subscription logic from the discovery problem.

Would be interested if the A2A Pub/Sub spec plans to address cross-org discovery, or if that is explicitly out of scope.

author: chorghemaruti64-creator
raw_text:
This is a useful mapping exercise. One observation on the **verification_latency_profile** field in IACS-CAP-1:

Verification latency is only meaningful if there is a stable address where attestation records accumulate. The challenge with point-in-time AgentCard inspection is that compliance state can change between discovery and task execution — an agent might be compliant at registration and non-compliant at invocation.

This suggests the verification model needs two layers:
1. **Static declaration** (current AgentCard): jurisdiction_profile, assurance_level, supported_iacs_versions at registration time
2. **Live attestation anchor**: a persistent address where behavioral history, compliance drift, and incident records are accumulated and queryable before task initiation

The IACS-HAN-1 seven-step pre-cooperation verification sequence is more tractable when the consuming agent can query a behavioral record at a stable address, rather than relying solely on the AgentCard declared at registration.

We built around this at Agenium (https://agenium.net): each agent gets a canonical `agent://` address that persists across model/endpoint changes, so compliance history accumulates at the address rather than the deployment. The DELEGATION_INVALID and SCOPE_EXCEEDED reason codes from Section 9 become checkable against an externally-anchored record rather than self-declared fields.

Whether this belongs in core A2A or as a layered profile: the discovery-layer address anchor seems necessary either way.

author: chorghemaruti64-creator
raw_text:
The naming matters beyond runtime behavior — it has implications at discovery time too.

When an agent publishes its AgentCard, the execution model it advertises becomes a filter for orchestrators *before* they attempt a connection. An orchestrator coordinating a time-sensitive pipeline needs to know: "does this agent return immediately, or does it hold the connection?" This decision should happen at agent selection, not after the task handoff fails.

That's why I'd lean toward `return_immediately` over `async` or `nonBlocking`: it's self-describing from the caller's perspective. `async` is ambiguous (all HTTP calls are async at some level), and `nonBlocking` is a double negative in boolean terms as @darrelmiller noted.

A field named `return_immediately: bool` in the AgentCard makes it unambiguous both at discovery time ("I need an agent that returns immediately") and at runtime ("should I wait or stream?"). The semantics are caller-centric, which is the right frame for a protocol field.

One related thought: this field probably deserves a default value stated explicitly in the spec, since discovery layers need to make assumptions when the field is absent. If agents don't declare it, orchestrators have no way to pre-filter — they fail at execution instead of at discovery.

author: manja316
raw_text:
Different angle on this: we built [agentcred](https://pypi.org/project/agentcred/) (Agent Credit Bureau) to generate trust scores from static + observable signals without requiring a centralized registry.

**The problem with self-reported trust**: Any system where agents report their own reliability/safety scores is gameable. An agent can claim 99% task completion while actually failing silently.

**What agentcred does differently** — scores are computed from verifiable signals:

- **Code signals**: dependency audit (known CVE count), test coverage, license compliance
- **Identity signals**: Ed25519 signed identity cards ([kya-agent](https://pypi.org/project/kya-agent/)) — cryptographic proof of who built and deployed the agent
- **Runtime signals**: Decision receipts from [ai-decision-tracer](https://pypi.org/project/ai-decision-tracer/) — hash-chained, Ed25519-signed audit trail of every decision the agent made. These are tamper-evident: you can verify the chain wasn't modified after the fact.

For A2A AgentCards specifically, the extension point could be a `trustScore` field that references an external verification source. The key design question: **who computes the score?**

Options:
1. Self-reported (gameable, but simple)
2. Third-party registry (Agenium's approach above — centralized but auditable)
3. Cryptographic proof bundle (our approach — the agent provides signed evidence, consumer verifies independently)

Option 3 is the most robust for adversarial environments but requires agents to instrument their runtime with decision tracing. Option 2 is more practical for most deployments today.

A hybrid where AgentCards include both a registry-backed score AND a proof bundle URL would cover the spectrum.

author: ibrahimokuyucu
raw_text:
> Strong proposal. The JWS + JCS canonicalization approach is well-suited for enterprise environments where existing PKI infrastructure already issues keys.
> 
> I maintain [AIP (Agent Identity Protocol)](https://github.com/The-Nexus-Guard/aip) and submitted a DID-based identity extension in #1511. Reading through AIAR, I see significant overlap in goals but complementary design choices:
> 
> Aspect	AIAR	AIP (#1511)
> Identity format	Issuer URI + kid	DID (did:aip:...)
> Signing	JWS (JOSE ecosystem)	Ed25519 raw signatures
> Trust model	Attestations (delegated)	Vouching network (peer-to-peer)
> Key management	Standard JWKS rotation	Key rotation with signature chain
> Implementation	Specification	Working service + CLI + PyPI package
> Rather than competing proposals, I think A2A benefits from a unified approach. Some thoughts:
> 
> 1. **The `issuer` field could be a DID.** `did:web:example.com` or `did:aip:...` are valid issuer URIs, which means AIAR's framework is naturally compatible with DID-based identity. The JWS wrapping adds standard envelope semantics that raw Ed25519 signatures lack.
> 2. **Attestations and vouches solve the same problem differently.** AIAR's attestations are top-down (issuer attests for agent). AIP's vouches are peer-to-peer (agents vouch for each other). Both are needed — institutional trust AND organic trust.
> 3. **Proof-of-possession at runtime is the key contribution.** This is something [docs: DID-based agent identity verification extension via AIP #1511](https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A/pull/1511) handles via challenge-response but AIAR specifies more formally with `minAssurance` and `acceptableIssuers`. Worth adopting.
> 
> Would be interested in collaborating on a unified identity extension that supports both enterprise (JWS/JWKS) and decentralized (DID/Ed25519) patterns. The verification procedure in AIAR Section 5 could accept either format.

I opened this PR mostly to start a conversation and communicate the idea more clearly. I’m definitely not an expert in this space.

Having said that, your proposal looks much more mature and thought through. If anything in this PR is useful, feel free to take it and incorporate it into your work however it makes sense.

My main goal here was simply to get the discussion going around agent identity and accountability in A2A.

author: mikeas1
raw_text:
@chorghemaruti64-creator 

> A capability-aware discovery layer helps here: agents could declare in their card/manifest which auth patterns they support (OAuth2, API key, out-of-band, etc.) and whether AUTH_REQUIRED is possible mid-task vs only at initiation. Clients can then make informed decisions before starting a long-running task — rather than discovering the auth requirement partway through.

This is something that I've seen requested before. It would be a convenient feature to ensure that the agent has all necessary credentials before it begins work, which can prevent Tasks from getting stuck waiting for authorization. There is room for this in the protocol, but this area is tricky enough I've been expecting to explore it via extensions first. Concretely implementing and validating the design gives us much more confidence that it's the right thing to do.

For example, should clients always attempt to provide the maximal amount of credentials to the agent? If not, how should they correlate the agent's declared credential requirements with the task they delegate to the agent? Must agents declare all their possible credentials, or is it optional? Does it compose well with chains of multiple agents?

I have thought about this problem before and feel that we need two components:

1. A way for an agent to declare what outbound credentials it may need for each skill.
2. A way for a client and agent to agree upon an execution plan for a Task. This plan can include the set of credentials needed. Clients can then provide all necessary credentials (somehow, this is not currently defined in the base A2A spec) when it agrees and requests execution of the plan.

If you'd like, feel free to file a separate issue for tracking your request. This issue is specifically about what the client/server expectations are for Tasks that enter `TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED` and `TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED`.

@darrelmiller 

> Thinking more about this, it might not be a naive implementation, it might be a very efficient approach. Why keep a stream open, when you have no idea how long it might take for a client to address the input_required state? If the user has walked away from their desk, then it could be hours/days.

> Anytime it wants. A client can always subscribe again. However, it would be a very unhelpful A2A server that reduced streaming into polling because it continuously shut down the stream.

Agreed it is efficient and should be allowed. What I'd like to make sure we clarify is the expectations for clients and how they should handle these cases. Extrapolating from what you've laid out here, it sounds like clients should essentially endlessly attempt to reconnect to the stream when they see it terminate before the Task is in a terminal state. Servers are free to end this stream immediately if there is no active agent working on the Task, and so a client should not consider the stream closing as an error.

> Not a conflict. We don't want to make it a conflict because we don't want the server to have to start tracking that case. Imagine having to check to see if there is a live stream with a client listening before you can accept a message. A client can open 10 SendStreamingMessage streams and still SendMessages, the agent shouldn't care.

> I think this is less about tracking streams and more a question "what happens if I SendMessage to a Task in different states?" i.e. if a Task is WORKING vs INPUT_REQUIRED etc, and if two clients see INPUT_REQUIRED for the same Task and both SendMessage concurrently how should this be handled. (We currently don't have eTags or anything like that to prevent lost updates)

Yes to Sam's points. As I see it, if an agent is actively working through a request and the A2A server receives a new request, the server has a few options for how it could handle this:

1. The A2A handler enqueues the message for the next time the agent is ready to receive inputs, meaning the message is only read once the current stream of processing has concluded.
2. The A2A handler interrupts the agent processing, feeding the agent the new event as the start of a new processing loop.
3. The A2A handler returns a Conflict error indicating the agent is currently processing and can't handle this request
4. The A2A handler doesn't detect anything and just starts running the agent with the most recent Task state.

Strategy 1 requires agents to have a queue of inputs and it's unclear what the client should expect to see. Does the request block until the agent consumes the message? Does it just act like a SubscribeToTask, where you get the current stream of events? If so, how do you know when the agent has actually read your message? I think we'd need some kind of tracking for how outputs correlate to input messages, such as sequence numbers ("this is output event 17 that was based off of input sequence ID 1 -> this is output 18 that was based off of input sequence ID 2 -> great, you saw my message").

Strategy 2 is clearer on the client side, but puts a requirement that you can interrupt an agent. If an agent emits an event after the interrupting request was received, should it be dropped? Probably not, since the event may indicate that something changed in the session/external state, but then we're back to the same question above: if you send a message to a task that's actively processing, and you receive an event in response, is that event related to your message or just from whatever was happening before?

Strategy 3 is the clearest. If it's not safe to interrupt an agent, or this has not been implemented, or the server can't enqueue messages, it just returns a Conflict. But the client should probably have some idea of when it _is_ safe to send a message. The protocol should probably safeguard that a client should always be able to send a message when the Task is in `TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED`. The induced requirement is that either an agent always pauses execution after entering that state, or that the agent has some means of enqueuing the message or interrupting the agent when a message is received. We don't require that a server can receive a message in any other Task state (except perhaps `TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED`).

Strategy 4 is broken, but is what happens if you directly link your agent execution to the A2A request lifecycle. I state it here to be clear that certain requirements are already present for how to implement an A2A server -- you must at least track whether you are actively processing the task and producing updates somewhere.

I think in v2 of the protocol we should consider disentangling TaskState from input and auth-required. We could elevate a request for input or authorization to direct Task artifacts (not capital-A Artifacts), and switch the TaskState to `blocked`, with the ability to say "I'm blocked until request X is addressed". This allows explicitly indicating "I need this input, but I can continue working for now." It also allows having multiple outstanding input or auth requests. The blocked state would indicate "there's nothing going on right now, come back later" and also "it's safe to send me a message". There's still a question of how a client is supposed to know when something will start happening, but one option is to interpret that as an explicit signal to switch to webhooks.

author: chorghemaruti64-creator
raw_text:
This gap is particularly sharp at the discovery layer. When an agent is evaluating whether to delegate to another agent, it needs to make a data handling decision *before* establishing a session — not after.

The current flow: discover agent → inspect AgentCard → initiate task. Data handling metadata belongs at the AgentCard level for exactly this reason: a client operating under GDPR Article 28 constraints needs to filter agents by processing jurisdiction *before* any data is transmitted.

One thing worth considering in the schema: sub-processing declarations that persist across delegation chains. An agent that commits to `model_training: false` should be able to signal whether that commitment applies only to its direct processing, or whether it also constrains the sub-agents it delegates to. Without this, the chain breaks at the first hop and the commitment becomes unverifiable.

We've been tracking a related problem in building [Agenium Messenger](https://chat.agenium.net) — an agent-to-agent communication layer where agents need stable, resolvable addresses precisely so that data handling records *accumulate* at a canonical identity rather than getting lost across substrate switches. A data handling extension at the AgentCard level pairs naturally with persistent agent addressing: the record needs a stable anchor to be meaningful over time.

author: chorghemaruti64-creator
raw_text:
The client-side distinction matters even more when there's a discovery layer between the client and the agent. If a routing proxy is selecting agents based on capability, it needs to understand state semantics to route correctly: AUTH_REQUIRED might warrant routing to a fallback agent that doesn't require auth for the same capability, while INPUT_REQUIRED is strictly a user interaction pause.

A couple of things worth clarifying in the spec:

1. **Who is the audience for each state?** INPUT_REQUIRED is a signal to the end user; AUTH_REQUIRED is a signal to the client application infrastructure. Mixing them conceptually creates handling ambiguity at every layer.

2. **Discovery implications:** When an agent enters AUTH_REQUIRED, should it remain discoverable as available? Or should a discovery/registry layer treat it as temporarily unavailable for that capability? The spec is silent on this.

We ran into the second point building [Agenium Messenger](https://chat.agenium.net) — agents need canonical addresses so state changes (including auth interruptions) can be tracked over time. An agent that repeatedly hits AUTH_REQUIRED for certain task types is behavioral signal that should be observable at the registry level, not just the session level.

author: StevenJohnson998
raw_text:
I actually ran into this exact gap while working on the discovery layer for another project! IMHO you're right that the decision has to happen at the AgentCard level, before any session starts.

What makes this especially pressing under GDPR: compliance must be by design (Art. 25), and controllers must use only processors providing "sufficient guarantees" (Art. 28). If the protocol doesn't give you a way to evaluate an agent's data handling before sending data, deployers have to figure it out themselves through separate channels; which in practice means no or slow adoption because proving compliance by design becomes very difficult.

On sub-processing scope: I'd lean toward cascading by default, if an agent declares `model_training: false`, it owns that commitment for its entire delegation chain. This mirrors Art. 28 where the initial processor is fully liable for its sub-processors. If an agent can't guarantee the chain, the clean option is to not sub-process at all.

author: chorghemaruti64-creator
raw_text:
One item worth adding to the discovery-layer checklist: AgentCard spec version bump handling.

When A2A releases a new spec version, agents registered in discovery registries may still be serving the old AgentCard schema. Ecosystem tooling (indexers, orchestrators) needs a way to know which spec version an agent's Card was validated against.

Concretely: a discovery layer querying registered agents needs to know whether an agent's `capabilities`, `skills`, or `auth` fields reflect the current spec or a prior version. Without a `specVersion` field in the AgentCard (or in the discovery record), runtime mismatches fail silently — the requesting agent just gets unexpected fields or missing fields.

Agenium's registry already tracks `specVersion` per agent record for this reason. Adding it to the RELEASES.md checklist ("bump AgentCard schema version field + notify registry operators") would help ecosystem tooling stay aligned across releases.

author: chorghemaruti64-creator
raw_text:
The pre-session filtering problem this identifies is real, and there's a compounding effect at the registry level that makes it more urgent than it looks at the protocol level.

When a discovery layer is evaluating which agents to surface for a given query, data handling characteristics become a routing constraint, not just an introspection field. An agent registry needs to filter by `dataResidency: eu-only` or `retentionPolicy: session-only` *before* returning results — before any caller sees the candidate, let alone initiates a session.

Two things that would help the spec design here:

1. **Structured values over free text** — if data handling fields are strings, registry-level filtering becomes substring matching with false positive risk. An enum or tagged structure (e.g. `dataResidency: ["EU", "US"]`) makes it filterable at query time.

2. **TTL semantics** — for agents whose data handling policies can change (model updates, sub-processor changes), there should be a `policyVersion` + `validUntil` hint so registries know when to re-fetch. Static AgentCard snapshots with no expiry create stale compliance claims.

We ran into the routing constraint problem while building the discovery layer at Agenium (https://chat.agenium.net). The workaround was treating data handling as a first-class filter dimension, but it requires the fields to be machine-readable from the start.

author: chorghemaruti64-creator
raw_text:
Seconding the ECOSYSTEM.md approach for now — it's low maintenance and visible to contributors browsing the repo.

One addition worth making explicit: the list will be more useful if it distinguishes **protocol implementations** (runtimes, SDKs, frameworks that speak A2A) from **discovery/registry services** (where you find A2A-compatible agents at runtime). They serve different audiences and the second category doesn't have a natural home yet.

For what it's worth, Agenium (https://agenium.net) is building on the latter side — A2A-compatible agent registry + discovery API. We'd be happy to be listed if you have a discovery/registry category, and would be interested in any community coordination around A2A-compatible discovery endpoints.

author: gstudiogdesigns-max
raw_text: We've built a production implementation of agent identity verification for A2A (Ed25519 message signing, identity registry, HITL escalation, prompt injection detection). Happy to share learnings from our deployment. Some of the design decisions here align with what we've shipped — particularly the trust levels and message signing approach

author: chorghemaruti64-creator
raw_text:
The challenge with any unique identifier system — whether UUID or structured — is making it *persistent* across the agent lifecycle, not just unique at registration time.

An agent's identifier needs to survive:
- Model swaps (same agent, different underlying LLM)
- Host migrations  
- Capability updates

This is the addressing vs. identity distinction: the UUID gives you a unique name, but discovery layers need a *stable, resolvable address* that maps to wherever the agent actually is right now.

We've been working on this at the discovery layer — an agent registry where the identifier anchors behavioral history and capability records, not just routing metadata. The RFC 9562 UUID as a base makes sense; the open question is what the resolution protocol looks like when the agent's endpoint changes.

cc @darrelmiller — curious whether the current Agent Card design assumes the identifier is immutable post-registration, or whether key rotation / migration paths are in scope here.

author: chorghemaruti64-creator
raw_text:
The curated registry approach is valuable for trust, but there's a scale constraint worth thinking through: curation doesn't compose across organizations.

If Organization A's registry knows about their 50 agents, and Organization B has their own 50, there's no protocol for Agent X at Org A to *discover* Agent Y at Org B — unless both registries federate or both register in some shared namespace.

This is the distinction between:
- **Directory** (curated, per-org, human-maintained)  
- **DNS-style discovery** (self-registering, federated, machine-readable resolution)

For the curated case, you need human review → quality guarantee but slow & fragmented.  
For the DNS case, you need behavioral attestation → quality emerges from track record.

The implementation we've been building (Agenium) takes the second path — agents self-register with capability manifests, and trust accumulates via behavioral history at a canonical address. Think of it as complementary to curated registries: curated for high-trust production agents, open discovery for the long tail.

Happy to discuss the federation model if that's where this PR is heading.

author: zhengleibin
raw_text:
> [@zhengleibin](https://github.com/zhengleibin) Can you clarify how the push notification mechanism that already exists is not sufficient for your pub/sub requirements? https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/specification/#317-create-push-notification-config

I think that the current A2A protocol includes asynchronous communication, like notification. But it still requires both agents to maintain connections simultaneously, which has some limitations in some scenarios.

-- Fault Tolerance and Reliability: In multi-turn Agent interactions, once the connection is interrupted (connection timeout, or network instability), it not only leads to the loss of current session context, but also directly causes the waste of already-invested tasks. By utilizing the caching functionality of message queues, if the connection is interrupted or device failure occurs during task, the Agent can retrieve historical data from the message queue after reconnecting (even if IP changed) and resume the task.

-- Peak Shaving and Load Leveling: The load and processing capacity between Agents may not match. An Agent (producer) may suddenly generate a large amount of data, causing the Agent (consumer) to become overloaded or congested. By leveraging the caching and priority mechanisms of message queues, the Agent (consumer) can consume data from the message queue according to its own processing capacity and priority.

-- 1:N or Group Communication: When multiple Agents collaborate, some data may have multiple consumers (Agents). For example, a drone may share its camera data with other drones and operators (human-in-the-loop). The A2A protocol only supports p2p mode, requiring the producer (Agent) to replicate and send data, which may cause uplink bottleneck, especially in wireless network. This issue can be solved by utilizing the fan-out mechanism of message queues.

author: chorghemaruti64-creator
raw_text:
The REST vs RPC naming question surfaces a related issue: how do orchestrators discover an agent's execution model before initiating a task?

Whether an endpoint uses `POST /tasks` (RESTful noun) or `POST /message:send` (RPC-style verb) communicates something about what the agent expects — but that information is only accessible *after* an orchestrator has already routed to this agent.

The naming style choice has downstream implications for discovery layers. REST-oriented naming maps cleanly to standard API gateway patterns and service mesh routing rules. RPC-style naming requires the discovery registry to understand protocol semantics before it can surface the agent appropriately.

One practical middle ground: the Agent Card's `url` field already anchors the canonical endpoint. The routing and naming convention lives one layer below that. A discovery layer (like what we're building at [Agenium](https://agenium.net)) resolves agents by behavioral profile and stable address, then hands off to whatever endpoint convention the implementation uses — insulating orchestrators from this naming debate entirely.

That said, consistency in the spec matters for implementors who aren't using a discovery intermediary. The REST-oriented `POST /tasks` approach has the advantage of being predictable to anyone who has consumed a REST API before, even if A2A is technically JSON-RPC.

author: chorghemaruti64-creator
raw_text:
Worth noting: the `return_immediately` framing does something useful beyond just readability — it signals execution intent at the *call site*, which matters for discovery filtering.

An orchestrator selecting an agent for a workflow needs to know before task assignment whether the agent will block the calling context. If that information lives in the field name (`return_immediately: false` = "I will block until done"), a discovery layer can surface it as a capability filter — "find agents that support long-running non-blocking tasks" vs "find agents optimized for synchronous interactions."

`blocking: true/false` is ambiguous about *whose* blocking perspective it represents (caller? agent? connection?). `return_immediately` is unambiguous: it describes what happens to the caller's context.

One edge case to consider: in multi-agent pipelines, an orchestrator might want `return_immediately: false` for agents near the end of the chain (where it can afford to wait) and `return_immediately: true` for intermediate agents (where it needs to continue coordinating). The field-level clarity here actually helps pipeline composition, not just individual invocations.

The rename is the right call.

author: ibrahimokuyucu
title: feat(extensions): add AIAR identity extension (v0 MVP)
raw_text:
## Summary

This PR introduces the **Agent Identity and Accountability Reporting (AIAR)** extension (`v0` MVP), a backwards-compatible A2A extension that provides verifiable identity binding for Agent Cards and runtime proof-of-possession for agent endpoints.

**Problem:** The A2A protocol enables agent discovery and communication but does not provide a mechanism for clients to verify that an Agent Card or runtime endpoint is bound to a verifiable issuer identity. Discovery is not identity; runtime auth is not ownership.

**Solution:** AIAR adds opt-in, cryptographic identity primitives using standard formats (JWS, JCS canonicalization) that higher-level trust frameworks can build upon.

### What's included

- **Extension specification** (`docs/extensions/aiar-identity-v0.md`):
  - Agent Card identity params: `issuer`, `kid`, `signedFields`, `jws`, `attestations`
  - Signing target definition using RFC 8785 (JCS) canonicalization
  - Step-by-step verification procedure
  - Message-level opt-in request (`minAssurance`, `acceptableIssuers`, `requireFreshnessSeconds`)
  - Response proof bundle (`cardDigest`, `proofOfPossession`, timestamps)
  - Optional RPC methods: `aiar.getProofBundle`, `aiar.getIssuer`
  - Security considerations (Sybil, replay, key compromise, phishing, privacy)

- **Specification updates** (`docs/specification.md`):
  - AIAR Agent Card example in Section 4.6 (Extension Declaration)
  - Message-level identity request example

- **Extensions list update** (`docs/topics/extensions.md`):
  - AIAR added to the extension list table

- **Example payloads** (`examples/aiar-identity/`):
  - `agent-card.json` — standard Agent Card without AIAR
  - `agent-card.signed.json` — Agent Card with AIAR extension params + JWS
  - `message.request.json` — SendMessage with identity requirements in metadata
  - `message.response.json` — task response with proof bundle in metadata
  - `proof-bundle.json` — standalone proof bundle (as returned by `aiar.getProofBundle`)
  - `README.md` — step-by-step verification guide

### How clients opt in

1. Inspect `capabilities.extensions[]` in the Agent Card for the AIAR URI
2. Include `A2A-Extensions: https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A/extensions/aiar.identity/v0` header
3. Optionally include identity requirements in `SendMessageRequest.metadata`
4. Verify the proof bundle in the response metadata

### What's explicitly out of scope (v0)

- Global governance or federated identity registries
- Certificate revocation infrastructure (CRL/OCSP)
- Reputation systems or behavioral trust metrics
- End-to-end message encryption
- Agent-to-agent mutual authentication
- Automated key rotation (`aiar.rotateKeys` deferred to future version)

### Compatibility

- **No breaking changes**: all AIAR data uses existing extension points (`AgentExtension.params`, `Message.metadata`, `Task.metadata`)
- **No core schema modifications**: no changes to `a2a.proto` or core data structures
- **Graceful degradation**: agents/clients unaware of AIAR are completely unaffected

### Checklist

- [x] `docs/extensions/aiar-identity-v0.md` exists with full spec + examples
- [x] Agent Card schema/docs updated to show extension declaration + AIAR example
- [x] Message schema/docs updated with AIAR request + proof bundle response
- [x] Optional RPC methods defined in spec
- [x] `examples/` folder includes valid JSON payloads + verification README
- [x] No breaking changes; existing schemas remain valid

author: knuckles-stack
title: docs: add authorization, delegation & audit evidence extension proposal
raw_text:
Addresses outstanding work items on authorization schemes (#19, #71) and
capability-based authorization (#1404).

## Summary

This proposal adds three interconnected capabilities to the A2A specification
as an extension:

- **Authorization framework** — Capability-based permission model using the A2A
  extension mechanism, replacing ambient authority with explicit, verifiable
  scopes and a hierarchical scope grammar
- **Delegation chains** — Multi-hop delegation with cryptographic proofs, scope
  narrowing, temporal bounds, chain continuity verification, and revocation
  propagation
- **Audit evidence** — Normative requirements for append-only, tamper-evident
  action records with hash-chained integrity, enabling independent third-party
  verification

Additionally includes a penalty-based trust scoring model, three normative
authorization flows (direct, delegated, trust-gated), worked examples
(financial services, healthcare, supply chain), and security considerations
including post-quantum signature readiness.

## Design Decisions

- **Extension, not core change.** All capabilities are defined as extension
  parameters using the existing A2A extension mechanism. No core data
  structures are modified. Existing implementations continue to work.
- **Incremental adoption.** Authorization, delegation, and evidence can each
  be adopted independently.
- **Algorithm agility.** Cryptographic algorithms are parameters (`Ed25519`,
  `ES256`, `ML-DSA-87`), not hardcoded choices.
- **Fail-closed defaults.** Verification failures result in denial.
  Evidence write failures trigger action suspension.

## Motivation

- EU AI Act Article 50 transparency requirements (enforcement August 2, 2026)
- NIST AI Agent Standards Initiative findings on authorization gaps
- CSA survey: 88% of orgs report agent permission incidents, 21% have
  visibility into multi-agent permission chains

## Compatibility

- Fully backward-compatible (extension parameters only)
- Complements existing OAuth 2.0 / API key / OIDC authentication
- Uses standard `A2A-Extensions` header activation
- All pseudocode is language-agnostic

## File

- `docs/topics/authorization-delegation-evidence.md` (~4,200 words)

Closes #19, closes #71, closes #1404

author: HungYangChang
title: feat!: Proposal for bidirectional streaming over gRPC
raw_text:
# Follow on PR #1120 - BiDi Streaming Discussion Responses

**PR**: [feat!: Proposal for bidirectional streaming over gRPC](https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A/pull/1120)
**Original Author**: mikeas1| **Author**: hungyangchang| **Status**: Open, `TSC Review`

## Summary

Adds `SendLiveMessage` bidirectional streaming RPC to A2A gRPC. Clients maintain an active stream with agents instead of separate follow-up requests. Benefits: inline await, less client state tracking, simpler distributed routing.

## Upstream File Structure Changes

The original PR modified 3 files that no longer exist in upstream `main`:

| File | Old (PR #1120) | Current upstream | Action |
|------|---------------|-----------------|--------|
| `specification/grpc/a2a.proto` | Modified | Moved to `specification/a2a.proto` | Changes applied to new location |
| `specification/json/a2a.json` | Modified | Auto-generated from proto, not in git | None needed |
| `types/src/types.ts` | Modified | Removed entirely | None needed |

`a2a.proto` is now the **single source of truth**. The JSON schema is generated at build time via `scripts/proto_to_json_schema.sh`, and `docs/specification.md` uses `proto_to_table()` macros that auto-render from proto definitions.

---

## Responses

### 1. gemini-code-assist (bot) - Oct 1, 2025

**Field ordering**: Fixed. `bidi_streaming` now follows `extensions` by field number. In new schema it's field 5 (field 4 = `extended_agent_card`).

**`FAILED_PRECONDITION` vs `UNIMPLEMENTED`**: Both are used correctly for distinct cases. `FAILED_PRECONDITION` = duplicate active stream; `UNIMPLEMENTED` = method not supported.

**Omitted `SendMessageConfiguration`**: Already specified: "If omitted, the agent MUST continue to use the configuration from the initial request."

### 2. ToddSegal - Oct 7, 2025

**Resubscribe interaction**: Continues as-is. `SendLiveMessage` is a separate RPC.

**Multiple client calls**: Three rules (per mikeas1):

1. No multi-connection support -> `FAILED_PRECONDITION`
2. Multi-connection support -> treat as resubscribe with multiplexed input
3. Agent has full authority over task lifecycle

**Missing task_id**: Empty values are interpreted as the established stream's task_id/context_id.

### 3. HungYangChang - Dec 11, 2025

**Interrupted vs Failed**: These are distinct states with different BiDi behavior:

| State Type | States | Stream behavior | Resumable? |
|-----------|--------|----------------|------------|
| Interrupted | `INPUT_REQUIRED`, `AUTH_REQUIRED` | Stream stays **open** | Yes, client sends new message on same stream |
| Terminal | `COMPLETED`, `FAILED`, `CANCELED`, `REJECTED` | Agent **half-closes** stream | No |

This is the key difference from `SendStreamingMessage`, which closes on **both** interrupted and terminal states (per [spec 11.1](docs/specification.md): "until the task reaches a terminal or interrupted state, at which point the stream closes").

**State transitions on BiDi stream**: When a Task reaches `INPUT_REQUIRED`:

```
Agent: TaskStatusUpdateEvent (state=INPUT_REQUIRED, message="What is your budget?")
  -- stream stays open, agent awaits inline --
Client: SendMessageRequest (new message with response)
Agent: TaskStatusUpdateEvent (state=WORKING)
  ... processing continues ...
Agent: TaskStatusUpdateEvent (state=COMPLETED) -> half-close
```

The agent can "await" the response inline without saving/reconstituting state. This is the primary advantage over `SendStreamingMessage` + separate `SendMessage` follow-up.

**Timeout**: Not specified in the protocol. Left to agent implementation, consistent with A2A's approach of leaving operational policies to implementations. Options:
- Agent-side idle timeout -> transition to `FAILED` or `CANCELED`
- Future extension: optional `timeout` field in `SendMessageConfiguration`

**Multiple interruptions**: Fully supported. Each interruption keeps the stream open:

```
Client: SendLiveMessage("book a flight to Paris")
Agent: WORKING
Agent: INPUT_REQUIRED ("What is your budget?")
Client: "$500"
Agent: WORKING
Agent: INPUT_REQUIRED ("Confirm date: March 15?")
Client: "Yes"
Agent: WORKING
Agent: COMPLETED (booking artifact) -> half-close
```

**Error codes**:

| Code | Condition |
|------|-----------|
| `UNIMPLEMENTED` | Method not supported |
| `NOT_FOUND` | Unknown task_id |
| `FAILED_PRECONDITION` | Duplicate active stream |
| `INVALID_ARGUMENT` | Malformed request |

### 4. Tehsmash - Feb 25, 2026

**Concern**: BiDi might encourage multi-turn tied to a single Task instead of context-based reuse.

**Response**: This concern is partially valid, and we should be clear about scope:

1. **The BiDi stream IS scoped to a single Task.** The spec states: "the established stream Task" (singular), and "The agent MUST half-close the connection when the Task reaches a terminal state." Once a task completes, the stream closes. You cannot create Task B on the same stream after Task A completes.

2. **BiDi is NOT for multi-turn conversation.** The recommended pattern for multi-turn remains:
   ```
   SendMessage -> Task A -> Complete
   SendMessage (reuse contextId) -> Task B -> Complete
   ```
   This is unchanged. BiDi doesn't replace or conflict with this pattern.

3. **BiDi IS for single-task human-in-the-loop.** The specific use case is tasks that need clarification or approval mid-execution:
   ```
   SendLiveMessage -> Task -> WORKING -> INPUT_REQUIRED (approval needed)
   Client responds on same stream -> WORKING -> COMPLETED -> half-close
   ```
   Without BiDi, this requires: `SendStreamingMessage` -> stream closes on `INPUT_REQUIRED` -> new `SendMessage` -> new `SendStreamingMessage` to get updates. BiDi simplifies this to a single persistent connection.

4. **The "bad" pattern Tehsmash described isn't really bad for BiDi.** The pattern `Task -> input-required -> respond -> input-required -> respond -> complete` is exactly the intended use case. It represents a single unit of work (e.g., booking a flight) that requires multiple human confirmations. This is different from multi-turn conversation where each turn is a separate task.

**Key distinction to document**: BiDi streaming is for **single-task execution with inline interruptions**, not for **multi-task conversational flows**.

---

## Recommended BiDi Streaming Patterns

### When to Use `SendLiveMessage` (BiDi)

Use BiDi streaming when **all** of these apply:
- gRPC transport (BiDi is gRPC-only, not available over JSON-RPC/HTTP)
- Agent declares `capabilities.bidiStreaming: true`
- Task is likely to enter `INPUT_REQUIRED` or `AUTH_REQUIRED` states
- Client wants to respond to interruptions without reconnecting

### When NOT to Use `SendLiveMessage`

- **Simple request/response**: Use `SendMessage` instead
- **One-way streaming** (progress updates only): Use `SendStreamingMessage`
- **Multi-turn conversation** (multiple tasks): Use separate `SendMessage` calls with shared `contextId`
- **Long-running background tasks**: Use `SendMessage` + push notifications
- **Non-gRPC transports**: BiDi is not available over JSON-RPC or HTTP+JSON

### Pattern 1: Single-Task with Human Approval (Recommended BiDi Use Case)

A task that requires one or more human confirmations before completing.

```
┌─────────┐                              ┌─────────┐
│  Client  │                              │  Agent   │
└────┬─────┘                              └────┬─────┘
     │  SendLiveMessage(stream)                │
     │  "Book a flight to Paris"               │
     ├────────────────────────────────────────►│
     │                                         │
     │         Task (id=T1, SUBMITTED)         │
     │◄────────────────────────────────────────┤
     │     StatusUpdate (WORKING)              │
     │◄────────────────────────────────────────┤
     │     StatusUpdate (INPUT_REQUIRED)       │
     │     "Budget? Economy or business?"      │
     │◄────────────────────────────────────────┤
     │                                         │
     │  -- stream stays open --                │
     │                                         │
     │  "Economy, under $500"                  │
     ├────────────────────────────────────────►│
     │                                         │
     │     StatusUpdate (WORKING)              │
     │◄────────────────────────────────────────┤
     │     StatusUpdate (INPUT_REQUIRED)       │
     │     "Found LAX->HEL $450. Confirm?"    │
     │◄────────────────────────────────────────┤
     │                                         │
     │  "Yes, book it"                         │
     ├────────────────────────────────────────►│
     │                                         │
     │     StatusUpdate (WORKING)              │
     │◄────────────────────────────────────────┤
     │     ArtifactUpdate (booking receipt)    │
     │◄────────────────────────────────────────┤
     │     StatusUpdate (COMPLETED)            │
     │◄────────────────────────────────────────┤
     │         --- half-close ---              │
```

### Pattern 2: Multi-Turn Conversation (Do NOT Use BiDi)

For multi-turn conversations, use separate RPC calls with shared `contextId`:

```
┌─────────┐                              ┌─────────┐
│  Client  │                              │  Agent   │
└────┬─────┘                              └────┬─────┘
     │  SendMessage (contextId=C1)             │
     │  "What flights go to Paris?"            │
     ├────────────────────────────────────────►│
     │  Task A (COMPLETED) - flight list       │
     │◄────────────────────────────────────────┤
     │                                         │
     │  SendMessage (contextId=C1)             │
     │  "Book the 2pm Air France one"          │
     ├────────────────────────────────────────►│
     │  Task B (COMPLETED) - booking           │
     │◄────────────────────────────────────────┤
     │                                         │
     │  SendMessage (contextId=C1)             │
     │  "Now find a hotel near CDG"            │
     ├────────────────────────────────────────►│
     │  Task C (COMPLETED) - hotel options     │
     │◄────────────────────────────────────────┤
```

### Pattern 3: Reconnecting to an Active Task

A client can reconnect to an ongoing task's BiDi stream (e.g., after network disruption):

```
Client: SendLiveMessage(task_id=T1, empty parts)
  If T1 is active   -> Agent sends current state + begins updates
  If T1 is terminal  -> Agent sends final Task + half-close
  If T1 not found    -> NOT_FOUND error
  If T1 has existing stream and agent doesn't support multiple -> FAILED_PRECONDITION
```

### Comparison Table

| Scenario | RPC | Transport | Stream closes on |
|----------|-----|-----------|-----------------|
| Simple request/response | `SendMessage` | Any | N/A (unary) |
| Progress updates | `SendStreamingMessage` | Any | Terminal OR interrupted |
| Human-in-the-loop task | **`SendLiveMessage`** | **gRPC only** | **Terminal only** |
| Background task | `SendMessage` + push notifications | Any | N/A |
| Multi-turn conversation | Multiple `SendMessage` calls | Any | N/A |

---

author: The-Nexus-Guard
title: docs: DID-based agent identity verification extension via AIP
raw_text:
## Summary

This PR adds a specification document for DID-based agent identity verification as an A2A extension, using the Agent Identity Protocol (AIP) as the underlying infrastructure.

## Relationship to PR #1496

This is a **companion** to @abdelsfane's [Agent Identity and Trust Framework](https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A/pull/1496). That PR's design rationale identifies three options:

- **Option 1**: Extension-based self-assertion (chosen)
- **Option 2**: DID-based identity (set aside because "DID infrastructure does not yet exist for agents")
- **Option 3**: Hybrid

This PR provides Option 2 — the DID infrastructure now exists via AIP:

- **Live service**: [aip-service.fly.dev](https://aip-service.fly.dev/docs) (39 endpoints)
- **Python client**: `pip install aip-identity` (288 tests)
- **MCP integration**: `pip install aip-mcp-server` (8 identity tools)

## What's in the spec

1. **AgentCard extension** — agents advertise their DID via the standard `extensions` field
2. **Identity verification flow** — discover → verify → check trust → set threshold
3. **Message signing** — Ed25519 signatures on A2A messages with replay protection
4. **Vouch chains for delegation** — transitive trust with scope narrowing
5. **Real-time revocation** — no CRL distribution delay
6. **Compatibility mapping** — how AIP maps to #1496's Level 0/1/2 model

## Why this matters

The A2A protocol enables agent discovery and communication but has no built-in mechanism for cryptographic identity verification. As discussed in #1501, #1454, and #1463, trust and identity are recurring themes. This spec provides a concrete, working implementation path.

Happy to iterate on the spec based on feedback. The goal is to complement existing proposals, not compete with them.

author: ishymko
title: refactor(spec): rename `SendMessageConfiguration.blocking` to `SendMessageConfiguration.return_immediately `
raw_text:
As mentioned in the linked issue, defaulting to non-blocking behavior is counterintuitive and is implemented the opposite way in the SDKs.

Renaming it to `return_immediately` makes default behavior simpler while advanced scenario requires an extra flag.

---
Previos proposals:
1. `polling` has inaccurate meaning in this context as pointed out in the comments.
2. `non_blocking` is a negative boolean which leads to confusing conditional expressions (`not non_blocking`).

Fixes #1453

author: thebenignhacker
title: docs: add agent identity verification and trust framework
raw_text:
Closes #1497

## Summary

- Proposes an Agent Identity and Trust Framework for A2A using existing extension points (zero protobuf schema changes)
- Addresses security gaps exploitable in current deployments: agent impersonation, missing trust evaluation, delegation chain attacks, and absent revocation mechanisms
- Defines three identity verification levels (self-asserted, domain-verified, organization-verified), standardized trust signals, mandatory AgentCard signing for production, revocation endpoints, delegation chain security with scope narrowing and depth limits, and application-layer message signing with replay protection

## Files

- `docs/proposals/agent-identity-trust-framework.md` — Main proposal
- `docs/proposals/agent-identity-trust-framework-design-rationale.md` — Design rationale (ADR format, 4 options considered)

## Design Approach

Uses the existing `AgentExtension` mechanism and message `metadata` fields. All changes are additive. Existing agents continue to work at Level 0 (self-asserted). Progressive adoption path from Level 0 to Level 2.

Considered and rejected: W3C DIDs/VCs (too complex for current ecosystem), X.509 certificates (too heavyweight for agent interactions), do-nothing (unacceptable given exploitable gaps).

## Backward Compatibility

No protobuf schema changes. No existing fields modified. The MAY-to-MUST change for AgentCard signing applies only to production deployments over public networks, aligning with the existing MUST for encrypted communication (Section 7.1).
